estimates.outcome: Cross-culture essay similarity, all writing tasks
estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Mean cosine similarity of OpenAI text embeddings for every Indian-American essay pair on the same topic, pooled over all writing tasks within each AI condition. The specific embedding model is not named. Higher similarity means less diversity across people.
estimates.treatment_arm: Indians with AI x Americans with AI (cross-culture pairs, both writers had AI)
estimates.control_arm: Indians without AI x Americans without AI (cross-culture pairs, neither writer had AI)

sources.quote: Overall, 118 participants completed four tasks each, resulting in a dataset of 472 essays. Among these participants, 65 received AI- generated suggestions to aid their writing—36 in India and 29 in the US.
It shows that without AI, the mean similarity between Indians and Americans was 0.48 (𝑆𝐷= 0.11), but with AI, the similarity score rose to 0.54 (𝑆𝐷= 0.13).
revealed that this increase was statistically significant, 𝑡(6958) = −17.89, 𝑝< 0.001.
Further, the effect size of this increase (Cohen’s 𝑑= −0.44)

estimates.notes: This is the main full-sample cross-culture similarity contrast. It includes all participants but only cross-country pairs, not all possible pairs within each AI condition. The printed t statistic and Cohen’s d are negative although the AI mean is higher; their direction corresponds to No AI minus AI. Their signs are retained exactly as printed. The paper does not define the standardizer for d. SDs and the t test are over essay pairs, with repeated contributions from each participant and no participant-level clustering reported. Figure 6(b) plots confidence intervals of the arm means, but the endpoints are not printed and are not read from the figure. The combined pair count is not printed, so n_units is null; no count is derived from the degrees of freedom. The pooled No AI participant count is also not printed.

estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Logistic regression predicts Indian versus American authorship using OpenAI essay embeddings as features, fitted separately for the AI and No AI conditions. The specific embedding model is not named. The mean score is reported in percent; its observations are held-out cross-validation fold scores. Higher classification performance indicates greater distinguishability between cultures, used here as an automated measure of diversity.
estimates.treatment_arm: AI condition (Indians with AI and Americans with AI)
estimates.control_arm: No AI condition (Indians without AI and Americans without AI)

stats.difference_is: Unsigned decrease from No AI to AI, as printed: control minus treatment, in percentage points.

sources.quote: Overall, 118 participants completed four tasks each, resulting in a dataset of 472 essays. Among these participants, 65 received AI- generated suggestions to aid their writing—36 in India and 29 in the US.
On average, the accuracy decreased by 7.1 percentage points, from 90.6% in the No AI condition to 83.5% in the AI condition.
This decrease was statistically significant, 𝑡(38) = 2.25, 𝑝= 0.03, with a medium effect size (Cohen’s 𝑑= 0.71).
This resulted in a distribution of 20 accuracy and F1 scores in each condition, which we compared using an independent samples t-test.

estimates.notes: This is an output-based cultural-distinguishability measure, not a convergent test taken by participants. The classifier is a scoring method; it is not an AI-treatment regression, so regression is null. The independent-samples t test treats cross-validation fold scores as observations; unit and se_basis are set. No participant-level or participant-clustered uncertainty, fold-score SDs, SEs, or confidence intervals are printed. The printed t statistic and Cohen’s d follow No AI minus AI and are retained without reversing their signs; the standardizer is not defined. The total number of fold-score observations is not printed and is not computed by adding the per-condition counts. The pooled No AI participant count is not printed. Means remain in percent, with no conversion to proportions.

not_extracted.what: S1-O2: Within-culture cosine similarity for Indians and Americans separately, the country difference-in-differences, and the baseline country comparison
not_extracted.reason: Country-specific AI effects are subgroup results, and the interaction is moderation. Country was recruited rather than randomized. No full-sample pooled within-culture AI contrast is printed. The baseline comparison is between countries without AI. Extraction-spec rules 4-5; PDF p. 9, Section 4.2.1; PDF p. 10, Figure 6(a).

not_extracted.what: S1-O3: Direction of homogenization, with only the Indian cohort or only the American cohort receiving AI
not_extracted.reason: These complementary contrasts change AI availability in one country subgroup while holding the other country’s unassisted essays as a shared reference. Neither contrast uses the full sample of both randomized AI arms. Excluded under the full-sample/subgroup rule. PDF p. 10, Section 4.3.1, Direction of Homogenization.

AI-versus-No-AI patterns are reported separately by country and only plotted. Printed tests instead compare Indian with American essays within each AI condition, not randomized AI conditions. There is no full-sample AI contrast. TTR describes vocabulary within an essay, not diversity across different people. PDF p. 12, Section 4.3.5 and Figure 9(a).

open_items: Counts at random assignment, noncompletion, and exclusions under the lifelong-country-residence rule are not printed. Analysis required completion of both the writing tasks and the later survey; these requirements followed random assignment (PDF pp. 4-5).

The pooled No AI participant count is not printed. n_control is null for full-sample estimates rather than calculated from the study total or the country-specific counts; the printed country-specific arm counts remain in the study record.

The paper provides no participant-level SD or participant-level/clustered uncertainty for similarity or classifier outcomes. Similarity precision is over essay pairs; main classifier precision is over cross-validation fold scores. The paper gives no data or code link.
The total pair count, total fold-score count, and email-only fold count are not printed for their respective analyses. They are not inferred from degrees of freedom or computed from per-group counts.

Mean confidence-interval endpoints for cross-culture similarity are figure-only. Classifier-score SDs, SEs, and confidence intervals are not printed. The standardizer for each reported Cohen’s d is not defined.
Embedding-dimension ablation results are plotted without numerical contrasts; essay length is described only narratively. Their eligible full-sample outcome records contain null statistics.
The exact OpenAI embedding model and the release year of GPT-4o are not stated. The model year remains null rather than supplied from outside the paper.
The saved arXiv version was not compared with the ACM version of record. The citation record identifies a later publication version.

The screening form flags a prose-versus-table inconsistency in Indian public-figure choice. This subgroup outcome is not extracted, and no replacement proportion is calculated (PDF p. 13, Section 4.4.3; PDF p. 20, Table 7).
notes: Extraction date: 2026-10-09. The entire markdown conversion was read from start to end, including references and Appendices A-C. PDF text was extracted with pymupdf for each cited page; Table 1 and Table 7 were also inspected using find_tables(). Only PDF page positions are used in locators; the saved document does not display a different printed page-number sequence. The screening form and citation record were used as maps, not as substitutes for the paper. No independent extractor file was read. Country is a recruited cohort, not a randomized treatment. The four cohort-condition arm names are retained from the screening form, while country-specific effects and country interactions are excluded under the explicit full-sample/subgroup rule. Email-only scoring remains full-sample because every analyzed participant completed that task. Classifier outcomes measure separation between cultures, hence diversity, not participant convergent accuracy. Writing-task eligibility rests on comparison of different writers’ outputs for similarity; no human rating of creativity is reported. No standardized effects, standard errors, confidence bounds, counts, proportions, or raw differences were computed. Source quotes are copied from the PDF text with whitespace collapsed; PDF line-end hyphens and mathematical characters are retained. Empty source-field lists provide evidence for narrative or methodological statements rather than unreported numerical statistics.
